Alexander II. Known as the Tsar Liberator, he embarked on the greatest period of Russian reform since Peter the Great, only to pay with his life for opening a window that the empire could not sustain. He inherited a humbled empire from his father Nicholas I and inherited with it an empire crying out for change.

His defining act came in 1861 when he issued the Emancipation Edict, freeing approximately twenty-three million serfs. It was the single most consequential act of his reign. The serfs received land and modest compensation schemes, but the redemption payments were onerous and the transition was chaotic. The edict delegitimized the landed gentry but failed to fully integrate the freed peasants into the economy, creating instead a new class of impoverished rural laborers. Yet across Europe, he was celebrated as a progressive monarch.

The Great Reforms of the eighteen-sixties followed swiftly. In 1864, he instituted legal reforms that were revolutionary for autocratic Russia: an independent judiciary, trial by jury, and secular law codes. In 1874, he reformed the military, replacing feudal conscription with universal conscription and modernizing officer training. He decentralized provincial administration through the establishment of zemstva—local councils—introducing limited self-governance at the provincial level. He also reformed education, expanding university access and easing censorship, which created intellectual ferment and student activism.

Militarily, he recovered from the humiliations of the Crimean War and fought the Russo-Turkish War between 1877 and 1878, defeating the Ottomans and supporting Balkan independence movements. He gained territory in Central Asia and the Caucasus, expanding the empire's reach. He even sold Alaska to the United States in 1867, ceding North American territory but gaining funds for domestic development.

Yet reform unleashed forces he could not control. Radical movements—nihilists, socialists, anarchists—proliferated, unsatisfied with gradual change. He faced numerous assassination attempts by the revolutionary organization Narodnaya Volya, the People's Will. In the eighteen-seventies, he attempted limited counter-reforms to reverse some of his earlier changes, which only provoked further radicalism.

On March 13, 1881, Narodnaya Volya terrorists assassinated him in St. Petersburg. His death marked the end of the reform era. His son Alexander III would respond by reversing nearly everything he had done, embracing reactionary consolidation instead. Had he lived and continued reform, Russian history might have unfolded differently. Instead, his death inaugurated three decades of stagnation that led directly to revolution. He remains Russia's most progressive tsar, yet his progressivism was incomplete and tragically fragile.
